progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: pathogen, host, the groups (bacterium, virus, protozoan, helminth) with these named cases: tuberculosis (bacterium), malaria and Plasmodium inside red blood cells (protozoan), the pork tapeworm hooked onto the gut wall (helminth), tinea (fungus), the COVID-19 virus and tobacco mosaic virus (viruses, made of genetic material in a protein coat, multiplying only inside host cells). From b02: germ theory, microbes come from other microbes, Pasteur's dust trapped in the swan neck (airborne microbes), Koch's tuberculosis work. From Year 11 Module 2: cell membranes carry proteins on their surface. Not assumed: modes of transmission, fomite, vector, droplet against airborne spread, fimbriae, receptor binding, entry against transmission adaptations, matching control to route.
progression.startsWith: Trace direct, indirect and vector transmission and the adaptations for entry and transmission. The video opens: In 1854, cholera was killing people in one London neighbourhood.
progression.stopsAfter: describing the chain a pathogen must cross to spread (leave, travel, enter); defining direct contact, indirect contact (fomites, water, food, air) and vector transmission, with named diseases for each, and distinguishing a vector from a fomite; explaining entry adaptations, which get a pathogen in and hold it where it enters (fimbriae gripping host cell molecules; viral surface proteins binding specific receptors; the tapeworm's hooks and suckers) and comparing bacterial and viral entry; explaining transmission adaptations (influenza triggering coughing and sneezing; *Plasmodium* in the mosquito's salivary glands, injected into the skin; tapeworm eggs and cysts in undercooked pork; tobacco mosaic virus surviving on tools); keeping entry and transmission adaptations apart in a comparison; matching control measures to the route; choosing the measure that breaks the link for a vector-borne outbreak and comparing two pathogens' adaptations.
progression.nextLesson: a classroom practical that models how one infection spreads through a group and how tracing contacts finds its source (route entry bio-m7-p01).

teaching.task: A pathogen can't survive in one host forever. How does it get out of one host and into the next, how is it built for each step, and how does knowing its route tell us where to stop it?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why a pathogen must travel to spread (it must leave, travel and enter; scene 2); why droplets count as direct and lingering particles as indirect (range and time in the air; scenes 3 and 4); why a door handle is not a vector (not alive; scene 5); why fimbriae help (grip, not washed away; scene 6); why a virus infects only some cells (its protein fits only some receptors; scene 6); why hooks matter (not swept out; scene 7); how each transmission feature moves the pathogen on (scene 8); why the control must match the route (scene 10). Visible case: the map cluster and the handle coming off; the lane changing per mode; droplets falling against particles drifting; the spike fitting one receptor; the scolex anchoring; four transmission cases; break marks cutting lanes. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scene 8 (four cases) is the densest scene, so each quarter dims as the next fills and only its amber tag stays bright.
teaching.conversationalApproach: In 1854 John Snow mapped cholera deaths around one London water pump and showed how the disease travelled without knowing its microbe, so the question is how a pathogen gets from one host into the next and how knowing its route tells us where to stop it. A pathogen has to leave one host, travel and enter a new one, and each link is a place the chain can break. The three modes of transmission follow one at a time with named cases: direct contact (tinea, HIV, close-range droplets for influenza), indirect contact through a fomite, water, food or the air (norovirus, cholera, Salmonella, tuberculosis and measles), and vector transmission by a living organism, with Plasmodium developing inside the Anopheles mosquito and a door handle shown not to be a vector. Adaptations are then sorted by job: entry adaptations grip and hold on (fimbriae, the COVID-19 spike protein binding its receptor, the tapeworm's hooks and suckers), and transmission adaptations get the pathogen out and across (coughing, mosquito saliva, tapeworm eggs and cysts, a tough tobacco mosaic virus coat). Knowing the route picks the control that breaks its link, from barriers to treating water to bed nets, and the memory aid is that every control measure breaks a link. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In 1854, cholera was killing people in one London neighbourhood. John Snow marked the deaths on a street map, and the deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. He didn't know which microbe caused cholera, but the map showed how it travelled: in drinking water. So how does a pathogen get from one host into the next, and how does knowing its route tell us where to stop it?
teaching.understandingCheck: 12a is an identify-and-justify item that meets the route's stop: Ross River virus after rain in a Queensland town, a mosquito-borne virus not passed directly between people; choose between isolating patients and draining and treating standing water. 12c is a compare item for B7-IQ1-04: Vibrio cholerae (pili, watery diarrhoea into water) against influenza virus (a surface protein binding airway receptors, coughing). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reason, givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ1-01: "describe a variety of infectious diseases caused by pathogens, including microorganisms, macroorganisms and non-cellular pathogens, and collect primary and secondary-sourced data and information relating to disease transmission, including: (ACSBL097, ACSBL098, ACSBL116, ACSBL117)", with its listed example "investigate modes of transmission of infectious diseases, including direct contact, indirect contact and vector transmission". B7-IQ1-04: "compare the adaptations of different pathogens that facilitate their entry into and transmission between hosts (ACSBL118)". This video covers the modes-of-transmission example (secondary-sourced: named diseases mapped to routes) and B7-IQ1-04. The epidemic example is p01 and g01; the microbial testing example is p02; the classifying example is b01. Verbs: "investigate" (examined, per the site's Compare model, as compare or classify a route with justification: scenes 2 to 5, 10 and attempt 1) and "compare" (scenes 6 to 9 and attempt 2: similarities and differences, not two descriptions).

design.visualSystem: One route chain board: two coded host circles (b01's `HostCircles` style), left "infected host" and right "new host", with a three-station strip between them: "leave", "travel", "enter". The middle station is a lane that changes per mode: in scene 3 a short lane with nothing in it (direct); in scene 4 a lane holding a painted object (door handle, pump, chicken) or drifting coded particles (air); in scene 5 a lane holding the painted mosquito. Adaptation plates attach to the "enter" station (teal tag "entry") or the "leave" station (amber tag "transmission"), so the board itself sorts the two kinds of adaptation. In scene 10 each lane gains a control plate and a coded break mark (a short scribble cut across the lane). Host circles are abstract and never become people: no people, hands, faces, patients, or coughing or sneezing figures. Droplets and airborne particles are coded dots leaving a host circle (abstract particles, not organisms). Real organisms, objects and tissues are painted plates; tissue blocks (skin) appear only as cut sections. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides the small grey station labels; tags fade when the next cue lands; lanes not being spoken about dim to grey.
